Fragmenta in epistulam ad Ephesios (in catenis)
Eph: Prolog
Ὥσπερ τοῖς Ῥωμαίοις ἔγραφεν, ὅτε μηδέπω αὐτοὺς τεθέατο, οὕτω καὶ τοῖς
Ἐφεσίοις, Ἰωάννου προλαβόντος καὶ τὸ κήρυγμα αὐτοῖς καταβαλλομένου, εὐκαίρως
παραινῶν αὐτοῖς μὴ κρατεῖσθαι νόμῳ. ἐπειδὴ οἱ ἀπόστολοι ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις
διάγοντες διὰ τοὺς ἀπὸ τῆς περιτομῆς πιστεύσαντας ἐτήρουν νόμον, εἶτα ἐπειδὴ
ἱκανῶς ὁ Ἰωάννης ἐθεολόγησε καὶ οὐδὲν ἐνέλιπε τῶν εἰς θεογνωσίαν κηρυγμάτων,
ὡς ἦν ἀνθρώποις χωρητόν, ἐπὶ τὸ παραστῆσαι τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως τὴν οἰκονομίαν,
ἔρχεται τὸ οἰκεῖον αὐτῇ μέγεθος καὶ διὰ ῥημάτων ἀξίως τῶν πραγμάτων 305
περιτιθεὶς καὶ τὸ δυσκολώτερον ἀναδεξάμενος· τὸ μὲν γὰρ τῆς θεότητος εἶχεν
οἰκεῖον τὸ ἀξίωμα καὶ ὡμολογημένον, τὸ δὲ τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως κατὰ τὸ
φαινόμενον ταπεινὸν ἀξίως διηγήσασθαι δυνάμεως ἦν πνευματικῆς. Eph 1,1
Κἀνταῦθα τὸ διὰ καὶ τῷ θεῷ προσήκει κατὰ τὸν Παῦλον, καὶ οὐκ ἠλάττωται πατήρ.
εἰκότως δὲ λέγει τὸ διὰ θελήματος θεοῦ, ἵνα δείξῃ ὅτι ὡς ἠθέλησεν ὁ θεὸς Ἰωάννην
εἶναι ἀπόστολον οὕτως κἀμέ. τοῦτο δὲ γράφει, ἵνα ἀξιόπιστα ᾖ τὰ ὑπ' αὐτοῦ
λεγόμενα. Eph 1,2 Εἰ ἑκάτερον καταχρηστικῶς εἴρηται, καὶ τὸ πατὴρ καὶ τὸ κύριος,
ὁμολογηθήσεται μείζων τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ υἱός, εἰ ὁ μὲν πατρὸς ἔχει ὄνομα, ὁ δὲ κυρίου.
ἀλλ' ὡμολόγηται τούτων τῶν ῥητῶν ἡ αἰτία· ἐπειδὴ γὰρ εἶπεν· πατρὸς ἡμῶν, πατὴρ
δέ ἐστι τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἵνα μὴ τὸ αὐτὸ ὄνομα καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ μονογενοῦς καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν
πιστῶν ᾖ κείμενον, ἢ τὸν υἱὸν καθελῇ παρὰ φύσιν, ἢ ἐκείνους ὑπὲρ φύσιν ἀναγάγῃ,
εἰπὼν πατρὸς ἡμῶν καὶ δεικνὺς ὅτι χάριτι ἡ προσηγορία, ἐπήγαγεν· καὶ κυρίου
Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ· οὐ γὰρ ἐνῆν κοινῇ φύσει τῆς προσηγορίας οὔσης κοινὸν εἶναι καὶ τὸ
ἀξίωμα. διὰ τί οὖν κύριος μὲν τούτων ὁ πατήρ, οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς κύριος τοῦ υἱοῦ,
εἴπερ καταχρηστικὸν ἦν τὸ τῆς προσηγορίας ἐφ' ἑκατέρων; Eph 1,4 Εἰ τοίνυν ἐν
Χριστῷ εἰς υἱοθεσίαν ὡρίσθησαν οἱ ἅγιοι, οὐ θετὸς ὁ υἱός, ἀλλὰ φύσει υἱός. Eph 1,5–
6 Εἰ κατὰ τὸν νόμον ἡ θέλησις ἐνέργειά ἐστιν, τίς ἡ εὐδοκία ἡ ταύτης τῆς θελήσεως;
οὐ γὰρ ἂν εἶπε «θέλησιν θελήματος». Εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ.
προλαβὼν ἤδη εἶπον ὅτι κατακοσμεῖ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ λόγον τῷ ἀξιώματι τῆς οἰκονομίας.
306 Eph 1,10 Ἐπειδὴ ἔπεσεν ὁ πλασθεὶς διὰ τῆς παρακοῆς, καὶ ἀσεβησάντων τῶν
ἀνθρώπων ἀπηλλοτριώθη τὰ ἐπουράνια τῶν ἐπιγείων, ἐλθὼν ὁ Χριστὸς πάντα
ἀνεκεφαλαιώσατο. καὶ τοῦτο μετὰ ταῦτα ἑτέρως φησὶν εἰπών· εἰρηνοποιήσας τὰ ἐν
τοῖς οὐρανοῖς καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. αὐτὸς γάρ ἐστιν ἡ εἰρήνη ἡμῶν, ὁ ποιήσας τὰ
ἀμφότερα ἕν, τοὺς Ἰουδαίους καὶ τοὺς Ἕλληνας, διὰ τῆς εἰς Χριστὸν πίστεως. Eph
1,11 Φανερῶς ἐνταῦθα ἄλλο ἐνέργειαν λέγει καὶ ἄλλο βούλησιν. εἰπὼν τοῦ τὰ πάντα
ἐνεργοῦντος κατὰ τὴν βουλήν, εἶπεν τοῦ θελήματος, ἵνα δείξῃ κεκριμένον τὸ
θέλημα. ἅπερ ἄν τις ἀπὸ βουλῆς καλῆς ἐβεβαίωσεν, ταῦτα κρίσει ὥρισται, λέγων
ἐχρήσατο ταῖς φωναῖς. Eph 1,13 Τῶν προεγνωσμένων, φησίν, ἐστὲ καὶ ὑμεῖς,
οἰκειούμενοι Χριστῷ δι' ὑπακοῆς καὶ τῆς ἐπὶ τῇ ἀκοῇ πίστεως καὶ τοῦ ἐπὶ τῇ πίστει
σφραγισμοῦ, ὅς ἐστιν ὁμοίωσις πρὸς Χριστὸν διὰ τῆς τοῦ πνεύματος μεταλήψεως.
παρὰ τίνος δὲ ἤκουσαν τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας; ἢ παρὰ Ἰωάννου τοῦ εὐαγγελιστοῦ;
ἐκεῖ γὰρ ἐκήρυττεν. διὸ καὶ ὑψηλότερον αὐτοῖς ὁ Παῦλος διαλέγεται ἐκ τῆς ἐκείνου
διδασκαλίας κατηρτισμένοις. Eph 1,14.17–21 Ἡ ἀπολύτρωσις τῆς περιποιήσεώς
ἐστιν· ἵνα γὰρ περιποιηθῶμεν καὶ οἰκειωθῶμεν τῷ θεῷ, ἀπολυτρούμεθα,
μεμνημένοι δὲ τοῦ αἵματος οὗ ἀπελυτρώθημεν καὶ τῆς οἰκονομίας πάσης. φανερὸν
ὅτι θεὸν τὸ κατὰ σάρκα τοῦ Χριστοῦ λέγει· οὐδαμοῦ γὰρ ἐνταῦθα τοῦ τῆς θεότητος
ἀξιώματος ἐμνημόνευσεν, ἀλλὰ τῆς καθ' ἡμᾶς οἰκονομίας ἥτις ὡμολόγηται τῆς
σαρκὸς εἶναι.
thought_title: Paul's timely letter and the dignity of the divine plan
orientation: Severian opens his commentary on Ephesians by explaining why Paul wrote to the Ephesians and how Paul's language honors both the Father and the Son.
pass_a_gloss: Just as he wrote to the Romans, when he had not yet seen them, so also to the Ephesians, John having gone before and the preaching being laid down for them, he urges them in a timely way not to be held fast by the law. Since the apostles staying in Jerusalem kept the law because of those who believed from the circumcision, then since John had sufficiently spoken of God and had left out nothing of the proclamations for knowledge of God, as was comprehensible for humans, to present the divine plan of the incarnation, he comes to the greatness proper to it and through words worthily of the matters 305 and taking up the more difficult part; for the part of the divinity had the dignity proper to it and acknowledged, but to narrate worthily the part of the incarnation according to what appears humble was of spiritual power. Eph 1,1 And here the 'through' also belongs to God according to Paul, and the Father has not been lessened. And he says 'through the will of God' reasonably, in order that he may show that just as God willed John to be an apostle, so also me. And he writes this, in order that the things said by him may be trustworthy. Eph 1,2 If each is said by improper use, both the 'Father' and the 'Lord', the Son will be acknowledged greater than the Father, if the one has the name of father, and the other of lord. But the reason of these words has been acknowledged; for since he said 'our Father', and he is Father of Christ, in order that the same name may not be placed both upon the only-begotten and upon the faithful, either to pull down the Son contrary to nature, or to lead those up beyond nature, having said 'our Father' and showing that the address is by grace, he added 'and of the Lord Jesus Christ'; for it was not possible, the address being common in nature, for the dignity also to be common. Why then is the Father lord of these, but he himself not also lord of the Son, if indeed the address was by improper use upon each? Eph 1,4 If therefore in Christ the saints were marked out for adoption, the Son is not adopted, but Son by nature. Eph 1,5–6 If according to the law the willing is an activity, what is the good pleasure of this willing? For he would not have said 'willing of will'. For praise of the glory of his grace. Having anticipated, I already said that he adorns his own word with the dignity of the divine plan. 306 Eph 1,10 Since the one formed fell through disobedience, and when humans acted impiously the heavenly things were alienated from the earthly things, Christ came and brought together all things. And this after these things he says in another way, saying: having made peace in the things in the heavens and the things on the earth. For he himself is our peace, the one who made both things one, the Jews and the Greeks, through faith in Christ. Eph 1,11 Clearly here he says one thing is activity and another is counsel. Having said 'of the one who works all things according to counsel', he said 'of his will', in order that he may show the will as decided. Whatever things someone would have confirmed from good counsel, these things have been marked out by judgment, he used the words saying. Eph 1,13 Of the foreknown, he says, you also are, being made at home with Christ through obedience and the faith upon hearing and the sealing upon faith, which is likeness to Christ through the partaking of the Spirit. And from whom did they hear the word of truth? Or from John the evangelist? For there he was preaching. Therefore Paul also speaks with them in a more elevated way, they having been equipped from his teaching. Eph 1,14.17–21 Redemption means being acquired as God's possession; for in order that we may be possessed and made at home with God, we are redeemed, remembering the blood by which we were redeemed and the whole divine plan. It is clear that he is here calling Christ God according to the flesh; for nowhere here did he mention the dignity of the divinity, but the divine plan according to us, which has been acknowledged to be of the flesh.

choices.why: Glossary requires 'divine plan' for God's saving plan, especially the incarnation.
Glossary requires 'law' for the Mosaic law.
Glossary votes for 'brought together' for Christ's recapitulation.
Glossary requires 'adoption' for the status of the saints in Christ.
Glossary requires 'redemption' for the deliverance by which believers become God's possession.
Glossary requires 'Spirit' for the Holy Spirit.

pass_b_english: Just as Paul wrote to the Romans when he had not yet seen them, so also he wrote to the Ephesians. John had gone before him and laid down the preaching for them, so Paul urges them at the right time not to be held fast by the law. The apostles who were staying in Jerusalem kept the law because of those who had believed from the circumcision. Then, since John had spoken of God sufficiently and had left out nothing of the proclamations leading to the knowledge of God, as far as was comprehensible for human beings, Paul comes to present the divine plan of the incarnation. He clothes it with its own proper greatness and with words worthy of the realities, and he takes up the greater subject. For the dignity of the Godhead had its own proper honor and was acknowledged, but to describe the incarnation worthily, which appears lowly, required spiritual power.

Here too the word “through” belongs to God according to Paul, and the Father is not diminished. He reasonably says “through the will of God,” so that he may show that just as God willed John to be an apostle, so also he willed me. He writes this so that what is said by him may be trustworthy.

Someone might object: if each term is said by improper use, both “Father” and “Lord,” then the Son will be acknowledged as greater than the Father, if the one has the name of father and the other the name of lord. But the reason for these words is acknowledged. For since he said “our Father,” and the Father is the Father of Christ, he did not want the same name to be placed both on the Only Begotten and on the faithful, either pulling the Son down contrary to nature or leading those others up beyond nature. So after saying “our Father” and showing that the title is by grace, he added “and the Lord Jesus Christ.” For it was not possible, when the title was common by nature, for the dignity also to be common. Why then is the Father Lord of these, but he himself is not Lord of the Son, if the title was by improper use in each case?
If then the saints were marked out in Christ for adoption, the Son is not adopted, but Son by nature.

If according to the law the willing is an activity, what is the good pleasure of this willing? For Paul would not have said “the good pleasure of his will” unless he meant to show that the will has been decided. “To the praise of the glory of his grace.” I have already said before that he adorns his own word with the dignity of the divine plan.

Since the one who was formed fell through disobedience, and when human beings acted impiously the heavenly things were alienated from the earthly things, Christ came and brought together all things. And after this he says it in another way when he says: “making peace between the things in the heavens and the things on the earth.” For he himself is our peace, the one who made both one, the Jews and the Greeks, through faith in Christ.

Clearly here he says that activity is one thing and counsel is another. After saying “the one who works all things according to the counsel of his will,” he said “of his will,” so that he may show that the will has been decided. Whatever someone has confirmed from good counsel, these things have been determined by judgment. He used the words in this way.

“You also,” he says, “are among those foreknown,” being made Christ's own through obedience and through faith in what is heard and through the seal upon faith, which is likeness to Christ through participation in the Spirit. From whom did they hear the word of truth? Was it not from John the Evangelist? For he was preaching there. Therefore Paul speaks with them at a higher level, since they have been equipped by his teaching.

Redemption means being acquired as God's possession. For in order that we may be possessed and made God's own, we are redeemed, remembering the blood by which we were redeemed and the whole divine plan. It is clear that he is here calling Christ God according to the flesh. For nowhere here does he mention the dignity of the Godhead, but the divine plan that is ours, which is acknowledged to belong to the flesh.

problems.quote: John had gone before them
problems.why: John went before Paul, not 'before them' (Ephesians).
problems.fix: John had gone before him

problems.quote: the one who works all things according to the counsel
problems.source_quote: τοῦ τὰ πάντα ἐνεργοῦντος κατὰ τὴν βουλήν
problems.why: Missing 'of his will' at the end - the citation is incomplete. 'According to the counsel' needs 'of his will' to complete the lemma.
problems.fix: the one who works all things according to the counsel of his will
problems.ruling: Source says τοῦ θελήματος after βουλήν; English omits 'of his will,' truncating the biblical citation and losing meaning.

problems.quote: he calls the Christ according to the flesh God
problems.source_quote: θεὸν τὸ κατὰ σάρκα τοῦ Χριστοῦ λέγει
problems.why: Word order: 'he calls the one according to the flesh of Christ God' or 'he calls God the one who is Christ according to the flesh'. The English 'the Christ according to the flesh God' is garbled.
problems.fix: he calls God the one who is Christ according to the flesh
problems.ruling: θεὸν τὸ κατὰ σάρκα τοῦ Χριστοῦ λέγει means 'he calls God the one who is Christ according to the flesh'; English word order garbles the meaning.

edits.old: the one who works all things according to the counsel
edits.new: the one who works all things according to the counsel of his will

edits.old: he calls the Christ according to the flesh God
edits.new: he calls God the one who is Christ according to the flesh

problems.quote: divine plan
problems.why: Same Greek oikonomia; reader may not connect 'divine plan' with 'Lord's divine plan' as same concept.
problems.fix: Consistently translate as 'divine plan' or add note.

problems.quote: brought together
problems.why: Same concept of cosmic unity; 'brought together' and 'reconcile' may seem distinct to reader.
problems.fix: Use 'reconcile/unite' consistently or note equivalence.

problems.quote: If each term is said by misuse
problems.why: Unclear if Severianus speaks, quotes opponent, or paraphrases Paul; no quotation marks.
problems.fix: Identify as Severianus's argument against imagined opponent.

problems.quote: If then the saints were marked out
problems.why: Conditional 'if' without clear antecedent; reader cannot tell if this is Paul's words, Severianus's inference, or hypothetical opponent.
problems.fix: Clarify: Severianus draws inference from Ephesians 1:5.

problems.quote: If each term is said by misuse—both "Father" and "Lord"—then the Son will be acknowledged as greater than the Father, if the one has the name of father and the other the name of lord.
problems.why: Self-contradictory or elliptical; argument structure collapses without more context.
problems.fix: Supply missing premise or note lacuna in fragment.

problems.quote: The redemption is of possession. For in order that we may be possessed and made God's own, we are redeemed
problems.why: Circular and opaque; 'redemption is of possession' is not standard English theological expression.
problems.fix: Revise: 'Redemption means being acquired as God's possession.'

problems.quote: misuse
problems.why: Probably means 'metaphorical/improper use' (katachresis), not 'misuse' as error; distorts theological argument.
problems.fix: Translate as 'improper use' or 'figurative use' with technical note.

problems.quote: containable
problems.why: Not standard English; probably means 'comprehensible' or 'capable of being contained' (human capacity).
problems.fix: Use 'comprehensible' or 'capable of being grasped.'

problems.quote: the law of commandments
problems.why: Reader cannot tell if 'law,' 'commandments,' and 'law of commandments' are the same or different concepts.
problems.fix: Use one term consistently or define each at first use.

variants.text: our being under the law of commandments

problems.quote: If each term is said by misuse—both "Father" and "Lord"—then the Son will be acknowledged as greater than the Father
problems.why: Reader cannot tell if this is Severianus's own argument or an imagined opponent's claim being refuted.
problems.fix: Mark as a hypothetical objection: 'Someone might say...'

problems.quote: If according to the law the willing is an activity, what is the good pleasure of this willing? For he would not have said "the willing of his will."
problems.why: Sentence is circular and unclear; 'willing of his will' is a literal gloss that does not parse in English.
problems.fix: Paraphrase: 'If will is an act, what is its good pleasure? Paul says "the will of his will" to show deliberation.'

problems.quote: It is clear that he calls God the one who is Christ according to the flesh.
problems.why: Syntax is tangled; reader cannot tell who 'the one who is' refers to.
problems.fix: Rewrite: 'He is here calling Christ God according to the flesh.'

problems.quote: by misuse
problems.why: Greek 'kata chrēsin' means 'by application/usage,' not 'misuse'; current rendering implies error.
problems.fix: Render as 'by application' or 'by way of usage.'

The English uses 'improper use' for katachrestikos, 'grace' for chariti, and 'nature' for physis; these are the standard renderings and are clear in context.
The English does not contain the phrase 'God of our Lord Jesus Christ'; the source does not use that phrase in this section.
